hook_text: How does a charge push something it never touches? Physics' answer changed everything.
clip_script: Hold two like charges near each other and you get a push with nothing visible doing the pushing. No string. No contact. Just refusal. How? Here's the answer physics settled on: a charge never travels alone. It fills ALL the space around itself with an invisible cushion of influence — thick close up, fading with distance, never quite ending. That cushion is the electric field. A second charge doesn't feel the far-away first charge; it feels the cushion right where it's standing. To map it, carry a tiny positive probe around like a candle in a cave, and draw an arrow wherever it gets shoved. Arrows always flee positive charges and dive into negative ones — a positive charge looks like a sea urchin with its spikes out. How strong is a spot? Quote the shove per coulomb, like rand per kilogram at the butchery: 4 000 newtons per coulomb is a rating for the PLACE, no matter who visits. And when two charges both broadcast, every point adds up what it receives — arrows that agree gang up, arrows that fight cancel, and between two like charges there's one dead-calm spot where the field is exactly zero.
visual_style: A dark space with charges glowing and translucent cushions of light pulsing around them; a tiny probe candle tracing arrows into a sea-urchin pattern; two overlapping fields with a visible dead spot flickering to zero between like charges.
mood: Wonder with a practical edge — the invisible architecture of space made visible.
pacing: Mysterious slow open, brightening middle as the map fills in, calm precise landing on the zero point.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read the invisible map before the exam asks you to draw it.
